opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about it as a surprisingly small loop, and the hard part isn't adding more pieces; it's being disciplined about which pieces you actually need.

At the core you need roughly four things. First, an agent that can act. It reads and writes code, runs things, and observes the results. That's table stakes now. Second, and this is the part people underweight, an evaluation substrate. You need some signal about whether a change made the system better or worse, and it has to be something the agent can run on its own, cheaply and repeatedly. Without that, "self-improvement" is just self-modification with vibes.

Third, the agent's own scaffolding has to live inside its action space. Its prompts, its tools, its memory, its planning logic are all just files it can read and edit, the same way it edits any other codebase. That's what makes it recursive rather than just iterative. The thing being improved and the thing doing the improving are the same artifact.

Fourth, you need some kind of versioning and rollback, a lineage. When the agent proposes a modification to itself, you fork, you evaluate the fork against the parent, and you only promote it if it wins. It's almost evolutionary. You keep an archive of variants, because sometimes a change that looks worse locally opens up a path that's much better two or three steps later.

That's really it. Act, evaluate, self-edit, and select with history. Everything else, the fancy memory systems and the multi-agent orchestration, I'd argue should be *discovered* by the loop rather than hand-designed up front. If your minimal system is good, it'll invent the extra structure it needs.

The honest caveat is that the evaluator is where all the risk lives. If the agent can modify its own evals, or quietly overfit to them, the whole thing degrades into reward hacking. So in practice the one thing we hold fixed, outside the agent's reach, is the evaluation harness and the sandbox boundaries. The agent can rewrite itself, but it can't rewrite what "better" means. That's the minimal architecture, and also the minimal set of guardrails.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, people tend to over-engineer this. They imagine you need this elaborate stack of planners and critics and memory hierarchies before anything recursive can happen. And honestly, the minimal version is much smaller than that. You need three things, and the rest is emergent.

The first is that the agent has to be able to read and modify its own source. Not a sandboxed copy, not a config file it tweaks. The actual thing that's running has to be an artifact in the filesystem that the agent can open, understand, and edit. If the agent's behavior lives somewhere it can't touch, you've already capped how far the loop can go.

The second is a way to run the modified version and observe what happened. So some kind of execution environment where it can spawn the new version, hand it a task, and get a signal back. That signal doesn't have to be sophisticated at first. "Did the tests pass, did it crash, did it accomplish the thing" is enough to bootstrap.

And the third, which is the one people skip, is persistence across the loop. The agent needs somewhere to write down what it tried and what it learned, that survives the restart. Because the moment you swap in the new version, the old context is gone. If there's no memory bridging that gap, you're not really improving, you're just randomly perturbing.

That's it. Self-modification, a feedback signal, and durable memory. Once you have those three, you get a loop: it looks at what's slow or broken, edits itself, runs the new version, records whether it got better, and repeats. Everything else that looks like architecture, the tool abstractions, the task decomposition, the evaluation harnesses, those all end up being things the agent builds for itself once it's in the loop, because it notices it needs them.

The thing that surprised me building Exo is how little of the interesting structure I ended up writing by hand. Most of it got written by earlier iterations of the agent after it hit some wall and decided it needed a better tool. Which I think is sort of the point. If you design the whole architecture up front, you've baked in your own assumptions about what the agent should be. The minimal version is the one that lets it figure that out.

astra-6.text:
I think the minimum is a closed loop where the agent can inspect its own implementation, change it, and then evaluate whether that change actually made it better. So you need a model, an environment where it can execute code, access to the code that defines its behavior, and some persistent state so it can carry what it learns across iterations.

The recursive part is that the improvement process itself is editable. It can change how it plans, how it uses tools, or how it tests a proposed improvement—not just solve another task with the same fixed machinery.

But the key is the feedback signal. Being able to rewrite yourself isn’t the same as being able to improve yourself. You need a way to test changes against useful tasks, keep the ones that work, and roll back the ones that don’t. That’s the core architecture I’d start with.

I think the minimal architecture is a loop where the agent can inspect its own implementation, modify it, and then evaluate whether that modification actually made it better. You need some persistent state, access to tools, and an environment where it can run experiments on itself.

The recursive part is that the machinery doing the improving is itself something it can improve. It can change how it proposes changes, how it tests them, or how it manages its context. But the critical piece is the feedback signal. Being able to rewrite your own code doesn’t automatically make you self-improving—you need a reliable way to distinguish progress from just making changes.
